activity_context.topic_title: Integration by Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{21}{7-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{1-{u}^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡u+C \\  & =3\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}})+C\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x}{\sqrt{7}}|<1.$
